flashcard_questions.a: Data based on numbers, such as sales figures and percentages.
Data based on opinions and attitudes rather than numbers.
Numerical information from a business's own accounts and financial statements.
Information a business collects about its own products and how well its marketing works.
Information about the wider market a business operates in.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sixth company's market share when the five known segments total 76.3%?
What is the average monthly revenue when four months come to £1,900,000?
What does a gross profit margin falling from 45% to 38% tell a business?
flashcard_questions.a: Its cost of sales is rising faster than revenue.

flashcard_questions.q: What must always be included with a figure taken from a chart?
Why is financial data described as backward-looking?
flashcard_questions.a: It is a snapshot in time showing only what has already happened.

flashcard_questions.q: What qualitative factors does financial data fail to show?
How can financial data mislead the people who read it?
flashcard_questions.a: It can be manipulated to present an overly positive picture.

flashcard_questions.q: How is the UK's 65-plus age group projected to change by 2039?
What happened to average weekly earnings growth in 2008 and 2009?
Why did falling earnings growth reduce demand for non-essential products?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers had less disposable income to spend.

notes: 15 cards: 5 term→definition (quantitative, qualitative, financial, marketing, market data), 2 one-step calculations using the lesson's own figures (pie chart 23.7%, average £475,000), 4 limitation facts split one per fact, 4 interpretation cards using the lesson's real figures (45%→38% GPM, 65-plus projection, 2008–09 earnings, disposable income).
